1.pericope_label: Cry aloud, spare not: is it such a fast that I have chosen, a day for a man to afflict his soul

schools.summary: Presses both the philology and the psychology: the cry is with the throat at full strength, the devout phrases ring with incisive irony, and the fasting is a work-holy delusion behind which self-righteousness and unrighteousness are concealed.

Allows the external piety as real so far as it goes, or as a caution against being imposed on by appearances, while judging that they sought themselves and the honour of men rather than God and his glory.

Reads the devout phrases as pretence and the observance as a fast with nothing in it but dumb signs, and turns the reproof on modern national fasts kept with all the forms of godliness and not a particle of its power.

Sets conviction before comfort and requires the wound to be searched to the bottom, grants hypocrites the praise of whatever good they do, and hears Cain's anger in their complaint that the service went unaccepted.

debates.question: Is the daily seeking described in verse 2 a real devotion honestly acknowledged, or irony throughout?

positions.view: a genuine external piety, which may be granted its due praise even in hypocrites, though it covers a heart that sought itself
every phrase rings with incisive irony, naming one element after another of a devotion the people did not possess

debates.question: What is the pleasure found on the day of the fast?

positions.view: worldly business carried on as usual, with labourers pressed and debts exacted on the very day of release
either sensual indulgence or, more probably, the pursuit of one's own desires, since indulgence would not agree with the affliction they professed

outliers.reading: Alone leaves the received Hebrew for the Greek at verse 4, making the blow one struck against the poor and the question why they fast to God in such a manner, and showing how few letters separate the readings.
Alone explains the fast-day quarrels psychologically, unspiritual fasting fretting the nerves and embittering the temper until the disputes rival those of drunken men.

themes: Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins.

Yet they seek me daily, and delight to know my ways, as a nation that did righteousness, and forsook not the ordinance of their God: they ask of me the ordinances of justice; they take delight in approaching to God.

Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not? wherefore have we afflicted our soul, and thou takest no knowledge? Behold, in the day of your fast ye find pleasure, and exact all your labours.
Behold, ye fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness: ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high.

Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the Lord?

6.pericope_label: Is not this the fast that I have chosen: then shall thy light break forth as the morning

schools.summary: Locates the chosen fast in self-denying love rather than in abstinence, without letting the correction abolish abstinence itself, and reads the wartime emancipation and swift re-enslavement of the slaves as the standing pattern of the fault.

Takes the bread both literally and as gospel bread dealt to the hungry rather than consciences burdened with rites of men's devising, and reads the promised light as chiefly spiritual and still to come.
Makes the duty immediate and universal, the fast day's food given away and the neighbour treated as one's own flesh by a chain of substitutions, and arraigns the slave trade under the verse.
Reads the promises as mercy after long affliction, with righteousness going before and the divine glory behind, and finds the readiness of the answering voice the strangest thing in the passage.

debates.question: Is the promised light temporal prosperity or spiritual blessing still to come?

positions.view: happiness and prosperity plainly, breaking through difficulty as the sun pierces a cloud, and mercy restored after long affliction
chiefly spiritual and future, the gospel shining out in all the world when persecution gives way to love
images heaped together to paint the fulness of blessing following the renunciation of the old selfishness

debates.question: Who are the poor that are cast out, and how far does one's own flesh reach?

positions.view: every kind of homelessness, tenants evicted, debtors, slaves fleeing cruelty, the persecuted, perhaps political refugees; and the flesh extends from suffering Israelites to all suffering humanity
wanderers with no abiding place, and no confining of the flesh to kindred, since we can look on no man without contemplating our own
the poor sheltered in one's own house as guests, with the relief of one's own decayed family a first obligation

outliers.reading: Alone turns the loosing of bands on the slave trade of his own day, telling those who traffic in the souls, blood and bodies of men to cast off the mask of religion rather than deepen their perdition by professing the faith.
Alone makes the bread spiritual as well as literal, the gospel imparted to the hungry, and calls burdensome rites of human devising husks and not bread.

themes: Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?

Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?
Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the Lord shall be thy rereward.
Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity;

10.pericope_label: If thou draw out thy soul to the hungry: the repairer of the breach and the honourable sabbath

schools.summary: Works through the renderings, sympathy drawn out rather than substance ministered, the bones strengthened or made supple, thy business rather than thy pleasure, and the high places of the land rather than of the earth.

Runs the rebuilding through the returned captives, the apostles repairing the fallen tabernacle, and a future mission to places with no preaching and no church, and catalogues at length the objects in which the promised delight is found.
Weighs the readings closely and applies them sharply, guarding the sabbath from visits and country jaunts and putting the whole chapter to a contemporary national fast kept for conquest.
Identifies the day as the weekly sabbath rather than the annual atonement, reads its restraints strictly down to our own words, and makes the keeping of it its own wages.

debates.question: What are the paths to dwell in that the restorer restores?

positions.view: the streets of the city, flanked once more with houses on either side rather than roads running from one point to another
the highways between cities, long desolate and uninhabited and grown over with grass and weeds, made fit for travel again

debates.question: What is the pleasure forbidden on the sabbath?

positions.view: recreation and sport, visits and country jaunts, and living at large without the restraint of conscience
one's business rather than one's pleasure, the foot turned away as from holy ground no profane step may tread
unnecessary journeys and servile work, the duties of the day performed with cheerfulness instead

outliers.reading: Alone dates and names a contemporary instance, a nation fasting in 1823 to subjugate its neighbour and restore the inquisition, and asks whether that is such a fast as God has chosen.
Alone reads the drawing out of the soul as describing gospel ministers who impart not the message only but their own souls with it.

themes: And if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul; then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday:
And the Lord shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not.

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.

If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:

Then shalt thou delight thyself in the Lord; and I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father: for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it.
